stem.text: Experiments were carried out to determine the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis of a species of the unicellular protoctist, Chlorella. A cell suspension of Chlorella was used.
Carbon dioxide uptake was used as a measure of the rate of photosynthesis.

items: The suspension of Chlorella was illuminated at a light intensity of 3 lux for 20 seconds.
The carbon dioxide uptake by Chlorella was measured at the end of the 20 second period of illumination.
The experiment was repeated at 6 lux, 9 lux, 12 lux and in a dark room.
The suspension was maintained at a temperature of 20 °C.

stem.text: Use Table 7.1 to calculate the rate of photosynthesis at a light intensity of 6 lux.
Complete Table 7.1 by writing your calculated value in the space provided.

markScheme.note: The MS prints the whole completed table, with the 6 lux rate shown without its decimal point ("22"); the figure is 2.2, found as 44 ÷ 20 s, consistent with the other rows (e.g. 72 ÷ 20 = 3.6).

explanation.text: Rate of photosynthesis here is total CO<sub>2</sub> uptake divided by the time over which it was measured (20 s). At 6 lux: 44 μmol ÷ 20 s = 2.2 μmol s<sup>–1</sup>.

inferredMistakes.text: Dividing by 6 (the light intensity value) instead of 20 (the time in seconds), confusing the independent variable with the measurement period.

stem.text: Plot a graph of the data in Table 7.1 on the grid in Fig. 7.1 to show the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis.
Draw a curve and extend your curve to show what would happen to the rate of photosynthesis if the experiment is carried out at 18 lux.

stem.alt: A blank grid for plotting rate of photosynthesis (μmol per second, y-axis, 0 to 5 in steps of 1, finely gridded) against light intensity (lux, x-axis, 0 to 18 in steps of 2, finely gridded).

points.text: best fit curve drawn for plots ;
curve levels off from 12 lux to 18 lux
alternatives: curve continues up at smaller gradient ;

explanation.text: Plot all five (light intensity, rate) pairs from the completed Table 7.1, including the 2.2 value found in (a)(i), then draw one smooth best-fit curve through them (not straight line segments). Because the rate is already rising more slowly between 9 and 12 lux than between 0 and 9 lux, the extension to 18 lux should continue that flattening trend: either levelling off completely or still rising but at a reduced, smaller gradient. Either shape earns the mark, since the question only asks for a sensible extension consistent with the data's trend, not a single prescribed answer.

reasoningChain: Plot the five points including the value calculated in (a)(i).
Draw one smooth curve of best fit, not joined straight lines.
Extend the curve past 12 lux following the flattening trend already visible in the data.

inferredMistakes.text: Extending the curve as a straight continuation of the steepest early gradient (0 to 3 lux), ignoring that the rate is already levelling off by 9–12 lux.

stem.text: Suggest an explanation for the shape of your curve from 12 lux to 18 lux.

points.text: curve levels off from 12 lux to 18 lux because light intensity no longer limiting ;
temperature / carbon dioxide concentration, now limiting ;

explanation.text: At low light intensities, light is the factor limiting the rate of photosynthesis, so increasing it increases the rate. By 12 lux the curve is already flattening, which means light intensity has stopped being the limiting factor — supplying more light beyond this point no longer speeds the reaction up. Some other factor, held constant in this experiment (temperature at 20 °C, or the carbon dioxide concentration available to the cells), has now become the limiting factor instead.

reasoningChain: A flattening curve means the previously limiting factor (light) is no longer limiting.
Something else, held constant in this experiment, must now be limiting — temperature or CO2 concentration.

inferredMistakes.text: Saying photosynthesis has simply "stopped" or "reached its maximum possible rate" without naming a specific alternative limiting factor (temperature or CO2 concentration).

stem.text: In photophosphorylation, photoactivation of chlorophyll results in the synthesis of ATP.
Describe how photoactivation of chlorophyll results in the synthesis of ATP in photophosphorylation.

points.text: electrons travel along ETC and energy released ;
(use energy released) to pump H+ into thylakoid, space/ lumen ;
increases concentration of H+ / protons (in thylakoid space / lumen) / creates proton gradient ;
H+ / protons, diffuse through ATP synthase ;

explanation.text: Photoactivation excites electrons in chlorophyll, giving them enough energy to be passed into the electron transport chain (ETC) in the thylakoid membrane. As these energetic electrons pass along the ETC, they release energy at each step, and this energy is used to actively pump H<sup>+</sup> ions from the stroma into the thylakoid space (lumen). This raises the H<sup>+</sup> concentration inside the thylakoid space relative to the stroma, creating a proton gradient. H<sup>+</sup> ions then diffuse back down this gradient, through ATP synthase, from the thylakoid space into the stroma — this flow of protons through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis) provides the energy that drives ATP synthesis.

reasoningChain: Electrons release energy passing along the electron transport chain.
That energy pumps H+ into the thylakoid space, building a proton gradient.
H+ diffuses back through ATP synthase into the stroma (chemiosmosis), powering ATP synthesis.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing H+ as moving into the thylakoid space by diffusion down a gradient, rather than being actively pumped there using the energy released by the ETC — the pumping step is what builds the gradient in the first place.
